newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-FRANCE FIGHT BACK TO REACH FINAL.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-FRANCE FIGHT BACK TO REACH FINAL.

text.p: France reached their second Davis Cup final in six years on Sunday when they completed a remarkable 3-2 comeback victory over Italy.
The French, Davis Cup winners in 1991, meet Sweden away in the final at the end of November.
France, 2-0 down after the opening singles on Friday, took the second reverse singles to clinch their world group semifinal when their number two Arnaud Boetsch beat Andrea Gaudenzi 6-4 6-2 7-6.
Boetsch needed five match points in the third set tie-break, which he took 10-8, to subdue the tenacious Italian number two after two hours and 36 minutes.
"The match summed up my recent problems on court but I managed to get through this time," Boetsch said.
French number one Cedric Pioline beat Renzo Furlan 6-3 2-6 6-2 6-4 in the first reverse singles to put France level.
The French began their comeback with the straight-sets doubles victory on Saturday of 1991 veteran Guy Forget and Guillaume Raoux over Gaudenzi and Diego Nargiso.
Pioline, ranked 17th in the world, said: "In the Davis Cup you always get a second chance. I served better today.
"It's easier for me to adapt to an excited crowd than to expect 6,000 people to adapt to me."

The shy and sometimes brooding Pioline did not manage to get the crowd strongly behind him on Friday but they lifted him from the start against Furlan and helped him give a much more passionate performance.
Pioline worked harder in the long rallies favoured by the Italian slow-court specialists and his greater mobility than on Friday kept Furlan on the defensive for most of the match.
Only five teams had previously come back from 2-0 down since the World Group was formally introduced in 1981.
Boetsch, on Friday erratic like Pioline, played a near faultless first two sets, hardly giving Gaudenzi a scent of a break point.
One break helped Boetsch win the opening set and he had two more on the way to the second.
Italy's captain Adriano Panatta said: "Boetsch, who's a great talent, played very well. But he got a bit nervous at the end. It wasn't easy for him."
Boetsch said he had played better than hs recent form on the tour "because in the Davis Cup it's a question of life or death."
In the third set Boetsch broke his Italian opponent in the first game then survived two double faults to retain his serve.
Gaudenzi finally broke Boetsch in the third game only for the Frenchman to break right back, when the Italian, having at last found his length, sent a passing shot wide.
The Italian's tenacity helped him break Boetsch again when the Frenchman served for the match at 5-4 and carry the set into a tiebreak.

Panatta was angered by a decision by the umpire to overrule a line call on a ball by Gaudenzi that looked good, and was confirmed as such in a television replay, denying the Italian a set point when the tiebreak stood at 7-7.
"The ball was good. It was an incredible decision, especially as it was the first overrule of the match," Panatta said.
"But let's not dwell on that ball. We might have won the set, but they played almost perfectly and were better."
France's captain Yannick Noah said: "In his (Panatta's) place, I would have got even angrier.
"Going to play the final in Sweden is good, it's another adventure after winning in Lyon in 1991."
Panatta added: "Well done France to have got out of a difficult situation with all the expectations weighing on them at home.
"I had hoped to win the first match today, but Pioline was very solid."
